```{r}
library(haven)
ess9 <- read_sas("ess9e02.sas7bdat")
ess9 <- data.frame(ess9)
source("Assignment6_prepare_ess9.R")
```

# Question 1

```{r}
library(corrplot)

corr_matrix <- cor(data_ess9)
round(corr_matrix, 2)
corrplot(corr_matrix, method="color", type="upper", addCoef.col="black", tl.col="black")
```

netincome & fairnetincome are  highly correlated (0.77)
age & timeinternet are correlated in opposite directions (-0.32)
number_household & age are correlated in opposite directions (-0.31)
netincome & polintr are correlated in opposite directions (-0.27) (with higher income people are more politically interested)
happy & polintr are not correlated (0.0)


# Question 2

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

eigen_decomp <- eigen(corr_matrix)
eigenvalues <- eigen_decomp$values

# Scree plot
scree_df <- data.frame(
  PC = 1:length(eigenvalues),
  eigenvalue = eigenvalues
)

ggplot(scree_df, aes(x=PC, y=eigenvalue)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept=1, color="cyan", linetype="dashed") +
  labs(x="Principal Component", y="Eigenvalue", title="Scree Plot")

round(eigenvalues, 2)
cumsum(eigenvalues) / sum(eigenvalues)


```
Keeping the two first principal components is adequate given for the plot, since the lie above the y=1 line. We can also keep the first three components, since the value for three is above the line (1.09) and left of the fallter part of the curve.

# Question 3


```{r}
pca <- prcomp(data_ess9, center=TRUE, scale=TRUE)
biplot(pca, scale=0, cex=c(0.3, 0), col=c("blue", "red"))
```

```{r}
loadings_df <- data.frame(
  variable = rownames(pca$rotation),
  PC1 = pca$rotation[,1],
  PC2 = pca$rotation[,2]
)

ggplot(loadings_df, aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, label=variable, color=variable)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(vjust=-0.5, size=3) +
  geom_segment(aes(x=0, y=0, xend=PC1, yend=PC2, color=variable), 
               arrow=arrow(length=unit(0.2,"cm"))) +
  coord_fixed() +
  xlim(-1,1) + ylim(-1,1) +
  annotate("path", x=cos(seq(0,2*pi,length.out=100)),
                   y=sin(seq(0,2*pi,length.out=100))) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  labs(title="Correlation Circle")
  #theme_minimal()
```

# Question 4

There are indeed 4 groups:
netincome & fairnetincome — pointing right on PC1
age — pointing up on PC2
number_household & timeinternet — pointing down on PC2
happy & polintr — at perpendicular nearly uncorrelated (not sure if this is a "group" in this context)

The correlation circle gives us a similar conclusion the one in question 1.


# Question 5

```{r}
scores_df <- data.frame(pca$x)

# Apparently 3 times the SD is common in statistics
scores_df$outlier <- abs(scores_df$PC1) > 3*sd(scores_df$PC1) | 
                     abs(scores_df$PC2) > 3*sd(scores_df$PC2)

ggplot(scores_df, aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color=outlier)) +
  geom_point(size=1.0) +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("grey", "red")) +
  theme_minimal()

outlier_rows <- which(scores_df$outlier)
data_ess9[outlier_rows, ]

mean(data_ess9$happy)
mean(data_ess9[outlier_rows, ]$happy)
```
The are some outliers (using a threshold of 3 times the standard deviation). They are high earners and they are a point happier on average than the rest.

# Question 6

```{r}
loadings_df <- data.frame(variable = rownames(pca$rotation), PC1 = pca$rotation[,1], PC2 = pca$rotation[,2])

ggplot(loadings_df, aes(x=reorder(variable, PC1), y=PC1)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title="Factor loadings - PC1")

ggplot(loadings_df, aes(x=reorder(variable, PC2), y=PC2)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title="Factor loadings - PC2")
```

On PC1:
netincome and fairnetincome (positive) (high loadings ~0.6)
vs
polintr (-0.4) (negative)

On PC2:
age (positive) (~0.6)
number_household, timeinternet, happy (negative) (~-0.3 to -0.4)

# Question 7

- PC1 can be interpreted as a socioeconomic axis. High scores correspond to higher income and more interest in politics.
- PC2 can be interpreted simple as a age axis. Older respondents (smaller households, less internet use) and younger respondents (larger households, more internet use).
